_about: Hand-compiled. Every figure carries a source; figures the article cites that could not be confirmed independently are marked asCited. Amounts are nominal in the original currency unless a source gives a modern equivalent.

reverse.name: Treaty of Nanking
reverse.detail: $6 million for opium destroyed at Canton, $3 million for Hong merchants' debts, and $12 million for the costs of the war Britain waged
reverse.why: Britain said China's suppression of the opium trade violated its right to trade, so China paid for the war fought to reverse it.

reverse.name: Haiti's independence indemnity
reverse.amount: 150 million gold francs, cut to 90 million in 1838
reverse.detail: About 112 million francs paid in indemnity and loan charges, roughly US$560 million in 2022 dollars (New York Times estimate)
reverse.why: A royal ordinance, delivered by a squadron of warships, made payment the price of French recognition. Haiti borrowed from French banks to pay, the "double debt".
sources: New York Times, "The Root of Haiti's Misery: Reparations to Enslavers" (2022)
LSU, France, Haiti and the Question of Indebtedness

reverse.name: British slave-owner compensation
reverse.payer: British taxpayers (and the enslaved, through unpaid "apprenticeship")
reverse.detail: About 40% of the government's annual income; raised through a £15 million loan in 1835 plus £5 million more. Nothing was paid to the people freed.
reverse.why: Abolition treated the enslaved as owners' property, so owners were compensated and the freed were bound to years of unpaid labour.

reverse.name: Indonesia's independence debt
reverse.detail: Debts of the colonial government, reportedly including the cost of Dutch military action against the Republic, assumed at the Round Table Conference. Sources give totals of 4.3 to 4.5 billion; one account puts repayments at nearly 4 billion before Indonesia stopped paying in 1956.
reverse.why: Taking on the colonial state's debts was a condition of the Dutch transfer of sovereignty.

spans.label: Repaid until Indonesia repudiated the agreement

corporate.intro: After decolonization, newly independent states nationalized foreign-owned concessions. Investment treaties and arbitration then let corporations sue states directly for compensation, which Anghie calls "corporate reparations".

compare.label: Everything the ICJ has ordered states to pay, 1949–2026
compare.note: Four awards: Diallo, Costa Rica v. Nicaragua, DRC v. Uganda (US$325.5 million), plus £843,947 in Corfu Channel (not included).

compare.label: Tethyan Copper v. Pakistan, one award (2019)
compare.note: US$4.087 billion in damages plus US$1.753 billion interest to the award date, over a mining lease that was never granted. Settled in 2022 through a new joint venture for the mine.

compare.label: The 12 largest investor–state awards
compare.note: 11 of the 12 went to fossil fuel or mining companies. The UN Special Rapporteur says the total likely exceeds all damages ever awarded to victims of human rights violations by all courts.

paid by governments to fossil fuel investors to date (2023)

cases.name: Rockhopper v. Italy
cases.text: Italy banned new offshore drilling near its coast; a tribunal awarded about €190 million (2022) for a production concession that had not yet been granted. An ICSID committee annulled the award in June 2025 over an arbitrator's undisclosed conflict.

cases.name: Eco Oro v. Colombia
cases.text: A majority found that Colombia's protection of a high-altitude wetland breached the treaty despite an environmental exception, though the damages phase awarded nothing.

colonial.name: Nauru v. Australia
colonial.text: Nauru sued at the ICJ over phosphate mining under the mandate and trusteeship, arguing breach of trust. After losing on most objections (1992), Australia settled in 1993: A$107 million plus A$2.5 million a year for twenty years, with Britain and New Zealand contributing.
sources: ICJ, Certain Phosphate Lands in Nauru

colonial.name: Herero and Nama genocide (Germany)
colonial.text: Germany acknowledged the 1904–08 genocide in political and moral terms and offered about €1.1 billion in development funding over 30 years, expressly not as legal reparations. Representatives of affected communities have challenged the joint declaration, and it was still contested in 2025.

colonial.name: CARICOM's 10-point plan
colonial.text: Caribbean states seek reparatory justice for slavery and native genocide. None of the ten points has been accepted; Britain declined to apologise at the 2024 Commonwealth summit.
